items.passage: Bao did not like surprises. As captain of the river freighter, he had found Wira curled among the rice sacks two days out, and now, docked below the terraced hills outside Hanoi, he had brought the boy home to eat because there was nowhere else to put him. Bao's mother set out bowls and chopsticks. Wira, from an island far to the south, hesitated, then began eating with his right hand as his family always had. Bao's mother watched a moment, then set down her own chopsticks and tore a piece of rice cake with her fingers. Bao felt the meal tilt on its hinge, the old customs of his house swinging open to make room for another. By the end, neither of them was eating the way they had begun, and no one remarked on it. Mist gathered over the terraces, erasing the lower paddies one by one.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the meal tilt on its hinge” most nearly suggests
options: a moment of clumsiness that nearly overturned the dishes on the table.
a sudden decision by Bao to send the boy away from his mother's house.
a shift in which the household's customs began to accommodate a guest.
an effort by Bao's mother to teach Wira how to use chopsticks properly.

items.passage: Dakar's Corniche was nearly empty at dusk when Yuto and Kwesi locked the shutters of their radio-repair shop for what might be the last time. Their oldest friend lay in the hospital above the promenade, and he believed the shop was thriving; they had told him so at every visit, describing customers who did not exist. Kwesi wanted to keep the story going a little longer. Yuto walked beside him along the sea wall and said nothing for a long while. He had begun to feel that their kindness had become a lantern without oil, something they kept holding up long after it had stopped giving any light. At the hospital stairs he stopped. He would tell their friend the truth, he said, and then they would sit with him for as long as visiting hours allowed. Kwesi looked at the sea before nodding. Fishermen were hauling their painted pirogues up the wet sand.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a lantern without oil” most nearly suggests
options: a costly gift that the brothers could no longer afford to give.
a secret that the dying friend had long been hiding from them.
a failing shop that needed repairs before it could reopen.
a comfort still offered though it no longer helped anyone.

a wool scarf, bright as warning paint,
in a city that rarely needs one.

a scanner for the shape inside a box.

and wears his smile like a borrowed coat,
buttoned to the chin against no weather.

all morning, the scarf stays on,
damp at the collar, itching, kept.
By noon the boy stops checking.
Gulls quarrel over a split crate of apples.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “wears his smile like a borrowed coat” most nearly suggests

an embarrassment Jakub tries but fails to hide from the other workers.
a plan Jakub has made to return the unwanted scarf to its seller.
a cheerful habit Jakub has shown every morning at the customs gate.

items.passage: We had planned the scattering for weeks: Salma would bring the boat, Ingeborg would read the letter, and I would keep the younger children away from the edge. Our grandfather had asked that his ashes go into the water off the Beirut harbor where he had fished as a boy, and every detail went exactly as arranged. The wind held. The letter was read without a tremor. Yet when we came back to the dock, Salma tied the rope three times, undoing and redoing the knot, and Ingeborg kept folding the letter into smaller and smaller squares. Our plan had been a bridge built perfectly to the wrong shore. We had prepared for every difficulty except the one of having nothing left to prepare. Along the breakwater, old men cast their lines and waited, rarely speaking.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a bridge built perfectly to the wrong shore” most nearly suggests
options: a project that failed because the weather on the water changed suddenly.
an arrangement that fully succeeded but did not reach the cousins' grief.
a disagreement among the cousins about where the ashes should be placed.
a journey that carried the family much farther than they had expected.

items.passage: Dario hung his uniforms on the rooftop line every morning at six, after our night shift at the bakery in Oaxaca, and I, Tendai, hung mine beside his. For months he had talked of quitting to drive a taxi with his cousin; he kept the license forms folded in his wallet and showed them to anyone who asked. That spring he spoke of it less. One morning I noticed he had begun pinning a second apron to the line, the white one the head baker gave only to those training for the ovens. He did not mention it, and neither did I. When I finally asked about the taxi, he shrugged and said his plans had gone out with the wash, faded a little each time until he could no longer remember their color. Below us the street vendors were unfolding their umbrellas, one stripe at a time.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “his plans had gone out with the wash” most nearly suggests that
options: his plans had been ruined by a sudden accident at the bakery.
he had deliberately thrown away the taxi forms he once carried.
his earlier intention had faded gradually rather than all at once.
he was ashamed that his uniforms had lost their original color.

items.passage: "Careful, that bow is older than both of us," Gunnar said, grinning, as Callum fumbled it beside the cafe's sugar bowl. Trains hissed beyond the Rotterdam windows, and the conductor teased the boy about his cold coffee and his crooked collar. Callum asked whose bow it had been. Gunnar's grin faded. He turned the bow slowly in his hands, thumb resting on the worn grip where another thumb had worn it first. He said that his teacher had played with it for forty years and had left it to him without a note. For a while he only watched the departures board. Then he set the bow in front of Callum and pushed it gently across the table.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From irritation to amusement as Gunnar forgives Callum's clumsiness at the table.
From playful banter to solemn reflection as Gunnar recalls the bow's former owner.
From anxious hurry to calm patience as Gunnar waits for a delayed train to arrive.
From formal instruction to open grief as Gunnar refuses to discuss his teacher.

items.passage: When I was nineteen, my stepfather and I worked the dark hours at Rivka's bakery in Haifa, shaping dough before the shutters rose. He had paid my first year of tuition with money meant for his own retirement, and neither of us ever spoke of it. For months I treated those mornings as a chore, sulking over the cold flour and his habit of humming off-key. Then one morning Rivka mentioned, offhand, that he had taken extra shifts all winter. I watched him fold the challah with his cracked knuckles and felt my impatience drain into something closer to awe. I began arriving early to light the ovens before he came. He never asked why, and I never explained.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From gratitude to disappointment as the narrator learns her stepfather resented the cost.
From cheerful curiosity to suspicion as the narrator questions Rivka's real motives.
From grudging irritation to humbled admiration as the narrator grasps his sacrifice.
From nostalgic warmth to sharp regret as the narrator recalls leaving the bakery.

items.passage: Two cups of cold tea sat between Meera and me on the reading-room table in Accra, where we had met every Thursday for three years to work on her novel. When the translation won the prize, I expected those Thursdays to feel like a celebration. For the first week they did; we laughed at the reviewers who praised my "invisible" English, and Meera read the congratulations aloud in a theatrical voice. But the publishers soon wanted a second book in half the time, and interviewers asked which of us had really written the famous closing chapter. Meera began correcting my drafts in ink instead of pencil. I began to dread the creak of the library door. We still met on Thursdays, though we spoke mostly about deadlines.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From weary routine to renewed excitement as the prize revives the partnership.
From resentment to forgiveness as Meera accepts the narrator's version of the chapter.
From quiet focus to open rivalry as Meera refuses to share credit in public.
From buoyant celebration to strained unease as success brings new pressures.

items.passage: Diesel and wet asphalt hung over the Taipei bus depot when Yuying finally brought Larissa down from the mountain trail. The hiker had been missing since dawn; the ranger had found her near a washed-out bridge and walked her six kilometers back. At the depot, other rangers crowded around, clapping Yuying on the shoulder. She shrugged them off, saying anyone could have followed the footprints. Yet when Larissa thanked her, Yuying recited, unprompted, the exact turns she had taken, the bridge she had judged unsafe, and the shortcut she had refused. Later, alone by the ticket window, she smoothed the creases from her uniform twice and checked her reflection in the glass before boarding the last bus home.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a rescue, presents a character's dismissal of praise, and then reveals details hinting at her hidden pride.
It introduces a hiker's mistake, explains its causes, and then describes how the hiker avoids repeating it later.
It recounts a celebration at the depot, then shifts to a flashback explaining why the ranger joined the service.
It presents an argument between two rangers and then shows how the hiker eventually settles their disagreement.

items.passage: Siti had not come to forgive anyone. She had come to the school music room in Thessaloniki only because Kostas, her father's old bandmate, had asked to return something. He stood by the dusty upright piano, turning his hat in his hands, while she kept her coat buttoned. __He set a cassette on the lid: her father's voice, singing a lullaby with her name in it.__ She had believed her father left without a thought of her. Kostas explained that the tape had been recorded the week before he went, and that he had been too ashamed to send it. Siti did not press play. But she unbuttoned her coat, sat on the piano bench, and asked Kostas to tell her about the band.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that Kostas, not Siti's father, was responsible for the family's separation.
It introduces evidence that challenges Siti's belief that her father had forgotten her.
It describes the music room's equipment in order to establish the story's setting.
It shows Kostas mocking Siti's reluctance to remember her father and his music.

items.passage: On my first visit back to Manchester after the move, Josiah took me to the bookbinder's workshop where we had apprenticed together as teenagers. He showed me the guest book we had bound for the owner's anniversary, still displayed on the front shelf. Everyone praised it, he said, every visitor for six years. I turned the pages and saw it at once: signature four was sewn upside down, a mistake I had made and hidden by trimming the edges. __Josiah ran his palm over the cover with obvious pride.__ I opened my mouth to confess, then closed it again. Outside, the rain started, and we stood under the awning eating chips from a paper cone.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Josiah has secretly known about the narrator's error all along.
It reveals that the workshop's owner has refused to display the guest book.
It suggests that Josiah is jealous of the praise the narrator received for the book.
It heightens the narrator's dilemma by showing how much the book means to Josiah.

items.passage: Three things I knew about Lorenzo before that night: he sold the best sfogliatelle in Naples, he never shared recipes, and he never seemed tired. At two in the morning I went to the all-night pharmacy for burn ointment and found him at the counter, buying the same thing. His forearms were striped with old scars from oven racks. The pharmacist greeted him by name and asked whether he had slept at all this week. Lorenzo laughed and said sleep was for bakers with smaller ovens. I had always believed his reputation came from some secret ingredient. Walking home, I passed his shop, lit and humming, the windows fogged, and I slowed my steps until I was well past it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Lorenzo?
options: Dismissive scorn for a rival she believes has cheated his way to success.
Lingering envy that grows stronger once she learns his secret recipe.
Detached indifference toward a baker whose work she rarely notices.
Grudging respect for a rival whose success she now sees was hard earned.

items.passage: Two tiffin boxes rested on the parapet of the stone bridge, one for Mohan and one for me, as they had every evening for thirty years. Below us the creek carried the smell of salt and diesel toward the sea. Mohan rarely spoke on these evenings, and I had long stopped expecting him to. That night he said only that the company in Pune had offered him the post. One of us had to stay with our mothers in Mumbai; we both knew it. I wanted to tell him that he deserved the post more than I ever would, that his quiet had always been a kind of steadiness I leaned on. Instead I slid his tiffin closer and said the dal was getting cold.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mohan?
options: Deep but unspoken affection for a friend whose departure he is prepared to accept.
Open resentment of a friend who is abandoning their shared duty to their mothers.
Amused impatience with a friend whose long silences have always irritated him.
Cautious suspicion of a friend he believes is hiding the real reason for leaving.

items.passage: When Lachlan finally carried the tin box up the lighthouse stairs in Galway, I had not spoken to him in four years, and our mother had been gone for two. The letters inside were hers, written to us during the winters she kept the light alone. I expected complaints; she had been a sharp, impatient woman, and I had left home partly to escape her. Instead the letters described the gannets diving at dawn, the exact color of the sea before a storm, and how she saved the best biscuits for when we visited. Reading them aloud, Lachlan's voice cracked. I found myself revising her as I listened, softening the hard edges I had carried. Outside, the lamp began its slow turn over the water.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her mother?
options: Lasting bitterness that the letters ultimately confirm rather than ease.
Growing tenderness as the letters complicate her earlier resentment.
Polite curiosity about a woman she barely knew as a young child.
Quiet guilt over having neglected her mother during her final years.

items.passage: After the irrigation pump exploded, Lars and Noor stood in the abandoned orchard outside Marrakesh, deciding what to tell his father. Lars, the landlord's son, suggested they say the pump had simply worn out with age. Noor, whose family rented the farmhouse, pointed out that he had run it dry all afternoon to fill a swimming trough. He argued that the truth would only get her father blamed for poor upkeep. By evening, they had written three versions of the story, each a little more careful than the last, and Noor insisted they keep the one that named Lars. He read it twice, then signed it. Overhead, the bare apricot branches clicked together in the wind like loose shutters.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how an irrigation pump was destroyed in an orchard outside Marrakesh.
To describe the orchard's decline after the landlord's family abandoned it.
To suggest that every accident has more than one equally valid explanation.
To show how Noor's insistence moves Lars from evasion toward responsibility.

items.passage: Gdansk in late October smells of wet grass and diesel from the shipyards, and that is where Milena found me, sitting on the bench beside the soccer field my brothers used to rule every evening. She had known my parents since before I was born, and she still called me Ksenia the goalkeeper. Our house two streets away was empty except for one thing: the cracked leather ball my father had signed for each of us. I told Milena I would throw it out, because keeping it felt like refusing to leave. She said nothing. She kicked it once across the darkening grass and waited. I ran after it before I knew I had decided to, and somewhere near the far goal I understood that a thing could be carried forward without becoming a weight. We walked home under the floodlights, the ball under my arm.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show how a friend's gesture altered the narrator's view of keeping a family object
To explain why the narrator finally agreed to sell her family's house after many years
To recall the narrator's childhood rivalry with her brothers on the neighborhood field
To argue that old family friends often understand grief better than close relatives do

items.passage: "Finish the balcony rail before the monsoon," Lakshmi said on the first morning I came to work for her at the shuttered cinema outside Thrissur. I was seventeen, and she was the last carpenter in the district who still built everything by hand. When I asked who the rail was for, she said the owner had been promised it years ago. But the owner, visiting in June, could not recall any such promise; the theater would reopen with or without a rail. Lakshmi only nodded and handed me the plane. All summer we shaped teak while the empty seats watched us. Only later did I see that she had kept the promise for its own sake, and for mine. On the last day she let me, Kenji, the apprentice who had once rushed every joint, set the final peg.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how the narrator came to resent a master who hid her true reasons
To convey how a forgotten promise became a lesson in valuing work for itself
To explain how the off-season shaped the business choices of a small cinema owner
To recount the narrator's long struggle to master traditional carpentry by hand

items.passage: Three stops, eleven minutes: that was how long Bruno had to talk with his cousin Caio each morning before Caio stepped off near the weaving cooperative in Lisbon. Their grandmother's old loom house, left to both of them, now had a buyer, and Caio wanted to sign by Friday. Only last week Caio had complained that the cooperative had outgrown its single cramped room. Today Bruno said nothing about the offer. Instead he pulled the bus to the curb one stop early, beside the cooperative's back window, where Caio's apprentices were threading a loom that had once stood in their grandmother's front room. Caio looked at the loom, then at Bruno, who kept his eyes fixed on the mirror. Walk from here, Bruno said. The air is good this morning.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Bruno most likely stop the bus one stop early?
options: He wants to avoid an argument by letting Caio leave before the offer comes up.
He is following a new route rule that requires him to stop near the cooperative.
He hopes the sight of the loom will lead Caio to reconsider selling the house.
He wants Caio's apprentices to see that he supports the cooperative's work.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 단서를 두 문장 이상 연결해야 하며 오답 중 하나는 결과를 동기로 착각하는 전형적 오독이다

items.passage: Years later, Karim would still describe the kitchen of that Bologna trattoria as a ship's galley: narrow, brass-railed, every pot hung where the sway of a sea might have flung it. He had come only to deliver flour. But he lingered in the doorway, watching Assunta correct her new daughter-in-law's pasta for the third time: too thick, too dry, too hurried. The bride said nothing and rolled the dough again. To the family at the long table outside, the two women looked like a perfectly matched pair. Karim saw instead that the young woman's hands were shaking, and that Assunta, without a word, slid the flour bin closer to her each time she spoke. Every correction was a rope thrown, not a blow. He left the sacks by the stove and never mentioned it to anyone.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a rope thrown, not a blow” most nearly suggests that Assunta's corrections are
options: a quiet form of support rather than an attack.
a test meant to push the bride out of the kitchen.
a habit she learned while working aboard a ship.
a public display meant for the family outside.
